abstract: Federal Reserve researchers synthesize multiple data sources to construct a composite indicator for tracking AI adoption across the US economy. The analysis integrates Census Bureau BTOS data (showing ~7% of firms using AI), American Time Use Survey (ATUS) data (showing 3.7% of workers reporting AI use on the job), and other federal surveys to build a multi-dimensional picture of AI diffusion. The composite indicator reveals AI adoption concentrated in information, professional services, and finance sectors, with substantial variation by firm size: larger firms (250+ employees) report adoption rates exceeding 20%, while small firms lag significantly behind. The paper represents one of the first systematic attempts by central bank researchers to develop a real-time monitoring framework for AI adoption, reflecting the Federal Reserve's growing recognition that AI diffusion speed and patterns have material implications for monetary policy, labor market analysis, and productivity forecasting.
keyFindings: Census BTOS shows ~7% of firms using AI overall, but adoption exceeds 20% among larger firms (250+ employees), revealing a stark firm-size divide in AI adoption.
American Time Use Survey data show only 3.7% of workers report using AI on the job, suggesting a significant gap between firm-level adoption claims and individual worker experience.
AI adoption is concentrated in information, professional services, and finance sectors, mirroring patterns seen in Eurostat EU data and private-sector surveys.
Small firms lag significantly in AI adoption, raising concerns about competitive dynamics and market concentration as AI-enabled productivity advantages accrue disproportionately to larger firms.
The composite AI adoption indicator developed by the authors enables tracking of adoption trends across multiple dimensions simultaneously.
methodology: Multi-source synthesis combining Census Bureau Business Trends and Outlook Survey (BTOS), American Time Use Survey (ATUS), and other federal statistical data. Researchers develop a composite AI adoption indicator that triangulates firm-level and worker-level data to produce a more complete picture of AI diffusion than any single survey provides. Published as a FEDS Note, May 2026.
qualifiers: Different surveys use different definitions of AI, complicating cross-survey comparisons. Self-reported AI usage by both firms and workers may suffer from definitional ambiguity. The composite indicator is a first attempt and may evolve as methodology is refined. Worker-level ATUS data capture time use but not productivity impact. The 3.7% worker usage rate may undercount AI use embedded in existing tools that workers do not recognize as AI.
